text: Annibale de Gasparis (Italian pronunciation: [anˈniːbale de ˈɡasparis]; 9 November 1819 – 21 March 1892) was an Italian astronomer known for discovering asteroids and his contributions to theoretical astronomy. Born in 1819 in Bugnara to Angelo de Gasparis and Eleonora Angelantoni, originally from Tocco da Casauria, he was the son of a doctor. He studied in the seminars of Sulmona and Chieti, developing a passion for classic novels and learning mathematics independently. In 1838, he moved to Naples to study engineering at the School of Bridges and Roads, today's Engineering faculty of Naples University, and the following year was accepted as a student at the Astronomical Observatory of Capodimonte by director Ernesto Capocci. He studied mathematics and celestial mechanics and published his first scientific paper on the orbit of the minor planet Vesta in 1845. For this work, he received the honorary degree in mathematics from the University of Naples as early as 1846. In 1848, he participated in liberal movements and, to avoid Bourbon repression, dedicated his first discovery, the asteroid Hygiea, made on 12 April 1849 using the equatorial telescope of Reichenbach & Utzschneider, to King Ferdinand II, naming it Igea Borbonica. In 1850, Capocci was dismissed as director of the observatory due to his involvement in liberal revolts, and de Gasparis refused to take over the position out of respect for his mentor and friend. In 1858, he was appointed professor of astronomy at Naples University. After Capocci's death on 6 January 1864, de Gasparis became director of the Astronomical Observatory of Capodimonte in Naples. Due to illness, he left the observatory in 1889 and moved to a country house near it. He married Giuseppina Russo in 1848 and had nine children, three of whom died in infancy. De Gasparis published more than 200 scientific papers on mathematics, celestial mechanics, astronomy, and meteorology. His name was occasionally written as Annibal de Gasparis. He visually discovered nine asteroids and independently discovered 14 Irene, though this discovery was credited to English astronomer John Russell Hind. He won the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1851 and received the Lalande Prize from 1849 to 1853. On 20 January 1861, he was appointed Senator of the Kingdom of Italy for his scientific achievements. He was awarded the Order of the Red Eagle and the Order of the Rose. The main-belt asteroid 4279 De Gasparis, the 30-kilometer lunar crater de Gasparis, and the nearby 93-kilometer long fracture Rimae de Gasparis are named in his honor.
